poem more carefully had he made a press copy of it. However, in the opening forty-eight
lines, which is the only part of TL in fair copy (Box 1 ff. 19r-20r), thirty-three lines are
enjambed and so are twelve of the sixteen tercets (including the first four of the poem),
which suggests that this looseness was a conscious decision. S.’s enjambment creates a
speed that provides TL with a remarkable narrative drive, as enjambed tercets force the pro-
gress of the sun’s rise, the wild dance, and the two triumphal processions. William Keach
has suggested that ‘In this kind of terza rima, rhyme defines a regular structural pattern
which is continually threatened with effacement as lines and tercets are denied grammat-
ical closure’ (Shelley’s Style (1984) 187–8). S.’s enjambment also softens the chiming triple
